title: Founder time management: why your best work keeps getting displaced
description: A practical calendar review for founders whose best hours go to approvals and rescue work. Match your capacity to the work that moves the business.
lead: Your calendar can be beautifully organized around the wrong work.
source: Adapted from the September 6, 2026 edition of Mastery in Motion, His calendar was working exactly as designed.
body:
A founder I worked with had an ambitious growth target and a carefully organized week. Meetings had boundaries. Thinking time had a place. Recovery was on the calendar.

Yet the work most likely to move the business forward kept slipping into the hours left over.

His clearest hours were going to solving, responding, and rescuing. He was highly effective at keeping the current operation moving. The next stage of the business was receiving whatever capacity remained.

That distinction changed where we looked.

What is your calendar producing?

When founders ask about time management, I want to understand the result the time is supposed to serve. An empty afternoon is useful only if it makes something important possible.

Start with one consequential outcome. Then ask: if you completed only three actions this week, which would move you closest to it?

For this founder, the answers pointed toward strategic thinking, partnership development, and high-value conversations. Those activities needed preparation and his better hours. Giving them a calendar slot was only part of the work.

The next question was what could move, shrink, or be handled without him.

Audit your best hours, not just your available hours.

Look at the previous five working days. Mark the periods when your attention and energy were most usable. Then look at what actually received them.

  • Progress: work that directly advances the outcome you chose.
  • Maintenance: work needed to keep the operation dependable.
  • Rescue: work that reaches you because ownership, capability, or a decision is missing elsewhere.

These are prompts for a review, not permanent labels for every task. An urgent client conversation can be the most consequential work of the day. The point is to see whether the pattern fits the result you say matters.

Ask what each category requires of you. Could a routine review happen when your concentration is less sharp? Could someone own the next decision with a clear standard? Does a difficult conversation need preparation before it needs another slot?

Protect the capacity the work requires.

My work in professional baseball sharpened a principle I also use in advisory: preparation has to match the demand. A schedule can contain all the right activities and still allocate effort poorly.

A founder's best commercial work might require clear judgment after a demanding morning, or the ability to listen carefully during a difficult negotiation. The surrounding load matters. So does the skill needed for the task.

If the work needs a capability you have not developed, protecting two hours will expose that gap. If interruptions keep winning because nobody else can decide, the useful change may be an ownership rule. If you arrive depleted, review the demands and recovery surrounding the work.

This is why I look across capacity, cognition, capability, execution, leverage, and context. The same crowded calendar can have different causes.

A related commercial-performance case.

In a separate earlier engagement, the work with David V. included protecting better hours for higher-value work, moving lower-value demands, and planning recovery and a shutdown. He later reported almost 200% of plan within three months.

The case includes a reconstruction of the working Performance Map and distinguishes the client-reported result from my account of the intervention. Read the case and its evidence limits.

Run one change for a week.

Choose one piece of consequential work. Give it a specific output, a place in your better hours, and a decision about what will move to make room.

For example: prepare the partnership proposal on Tuesday morning; move the routine review to the afternoon; agree which questions the team can resolve before escalating. This is an illustration, not a formula for every founder.

At the end of the week, review four questions:

  1. What was supposed to happen?
  2. What actually happened?
  3. What explains the gap?
  4. What will you change next week?

Record the output and the cost: work displaced, rescue required, and whether the working day ended where you intended. A fuller calendar is a poor substitute for evidence of progress.

What is currently receiving your best hours that no longer deserves them?

If the same work keeps returning to you, read The founder bottleneck. It looks at the dependence that a well-organized calendar can conceal.
cta: If your next stage of growth keeps receiving the capacity left over, we can examine what needs to change first.

title: The founder bottleneck: when your ability to cope hides the problem
description: When decisions and rescue work keep returning to the founder, better effort can hide a weak system. Find the dependence and test one change.
lead: High performers can make bad systems look healthy. The work gets done. The cost stays with them.
source: Expanded from a Mastery in Motion field note and the September 27, 2026 letter on the cost of compensation. The anonymized operator example draws on Marcus’s retrospective engagement record; no financial or health figures are included.
body:
The client stays happy. The deadline holds. Revenue arrives. From the outside, the business appears to function.

Look more closely at where the effort lands. You catch the dropped handoff. Rewrite the proposal. Answer the question somebody else technically owns. Finish your most important work after everyone else has stopped.

Your competence becomes part of the operating system. Eventually, people plan around it.

This is one version of the founder bottleneck: the business keeps reaching you because your ability to compensate has made the underlying dependence difficult to see.

Separate the result from what it costs to produce.

Professional sport taught me to look beyond the visible result. An athlete can keep performing while preparation, recovery, or the way the team works around them needs attention. A good outcome alone cannot tell you whether the approach will hold across repeated demand.

I bring the same question to advisory: what is required to keep producing this result, and who is absorbing the cost?

For a founder, that cost may be strategic work postponed, a team waiting for permission, or attention that never quite returns to home. If the scorecard measures only delivery, those costs can stay invisible.

Start by distinguishing the involvement that improves the result from the involvement that has become the default.

Find one recurring point of dependence.

Choose something that reached you more than once last week. A pricing approval. A client deliverable that needed rescuing. A decision the team could not make without you.

Ask what would need to be true for the next occurrence to move forward well without your involvement.

  • Ownership: does one person know the decision is theirs?
  • Capability: can they make it, and have they practiced?
  • Standard: can they recognize an acceptable result?
  • Authority: do they know the boundaries within which they can act?
  • Escalation: is it clear when your judgment is genuinely required?

Different answers point to different work. A missing skill needs practice. Unclear ownership needs a decision. A vague standard needs an example. More focus from you can leave each of those conditions unchanged.

What this looked like in earlier work.

In an earlier operator engagement, the recurring pattern was being pulled from strategic work into execution, mediation, and rescue. My retrospective account of the work identified unclear role boundaries as a useful place to intervene.

We worked on role clarity, decision trees, escalation rules, and boundaries around reactive requests. Later in the engagement, the client created one-page strategic plans across several businesses and began building tools for client management. Those are documented outputs in my account, not a measured reduction in hours or an independently established causal result.

The change was specific: define where the operator’s judgment was needed and give recurring decisions a way to move without automatically returning to them.

A decision boundary to make explicit.

Owner
Who makes this decision?
Standard
What does an acceptable result look like?
Boundary
What can they decide without you?
Exception
What must come back, and why?

Illustrative reconstruction of the decision-tree approach, not an original client artifact.

When expertise itself is tied to the founder’s time, the next change may be the delivery model. In a separate 30-day engagement, Jason F. and I worked on his capacity, commercial priority, and a structured offer he could test. Read the founder advisory case.

Check your part in the pattern.

Sometimes the team has learned that you will rewrite the work even when it meets the agreed standard. Sometimes answering immediately is easier than explaining the decision. Sometimes the work matters enough that you should remain involved.

The useful question is where your judgment creates value and where your habits create dependence.

Take a recurring proposal review. You might retain responsibility for unusual commercial risk while someone else owns routine proposals against an agreed standard. That requires a shared understanding of risk, examples of good work, and a way to raise exceptions. Simply asking the team to be more proactive leaves too much undefined.

This example illustrates the design of a change. The right boundary depends on your people, stakes, and circumstances.

Test independence without losing quality.

Choose one recurring decision. Agree who owns it, what good looks like, and when it should return to you. Try that arrangement for a week.

Watch both sides: how often you are interrupted and whether the quality of the work holds. Notice delays, rework, and exceptions. Time recovered without a dependable result is an incomplete improvement.

If quality drops, investigate why before taking everything back. The person may need a better example, more practice, or a narrower decision boundary. If interruptions remain unchanged, the agreement may not be clear enough to use.

Give the recovered capacity a purpose.

Reclaimed time can disappear into the next incoming request. Decide in advance what it should enable: a consequential commercial move, deeper work, or a more deliberate end to the day.

Review whether that happened. The objective is a business that performs with less unnecessary dependence on your constant intervention, and a life that receives more than whatever remains.

What is one thing someone else technically owns that you still end up touching?

To examine where the recovered capacity should go, read why your best work keeps getting displaced.
cta: If the business performs because you keep absorbing what the system cannot, we can identify the dependence and design a focused test.

title: How to think clearly under pressure: find what is driving the reaction
description: A practical way to separate facts, assumptions, and the demands of a decision when pressure narrows your view. From Marcus Lefton’s Mastery in Motion.
lead: Before you answer the message, understand the situation you are answering.
source: Adapted from the June 21, 2026 edition of Mastery in Motion, Before you know why. The example below is illustrative.
body:
A message arrives: “Can we talk about the proposal?”

You read it as dissatisfaction. Your attention moves to everything that could be wrong. You begin composing an explanation before you know what the other person wants to discuss.

The message is short. The situation taking shape in your mind is much larger.

This illustrative example captures a pattern worth noticing in consequential work. An interpretation can start directing your behavior before you have examined it.

Pressure changes the conditions for judgment.

Research reviewed by neuroscientist Amy Arnsten describes how acute, uncontrollable stress can impair prefrontal functions involved in working memory and flexible thinking. That helps explain why a person may have less access to their usual perspective under pressure. It does not tell us the cause of any individual's reaction.

In advisory, I want to understand the interaction: what happened, what you made it mean, the state you brought to it, and what the decision actually requires.

The aim is to make a response that fits the facts and the stakes. Sometimes that means acting quickly. Sometimes it means asking a better question before committing.

Separate the fact from the story.

Before responding to an ambiguous message, write two short lines:

  • What I know: the person wants to discuss the proposal.
  • What I am assuming: they dislike it, the relationship is at risk, and I need to defend it now.

Then ask what evidence supports the assumption and what information would change it. The concern may be justified. The exercise gives you a way to examine it.

In this example, the most useful next move could be: “Of course. Which part would you like to discuss so I can come prepared?” That question improves the information available before you invest in a response.

Look beyond the immediate thought.

If a reaction keeps repeating, the interpretation is only one place to look. Ask what else is contributing.

  • Capacity: are you entering these conversations already depleted?
  • Cognition: which assumptions are narrowing what you notice?
  • Capability: is this a conversation or decision you need more practice handling?
  • Execution: is there a clear next action, or are several unresolved tasks competing for attention?
  • Leverage: does this actually require your involvement?
  • Context: are the stakes and response time clear, or are you filling in the gaps?

A difficult negotiation may call for preparation. Repeated false urgency may call for communication agreements. An overloaded week may call for changing the load. The explanation determines which intervention is worth testing.

Use a short decision reset.

For a non-emergency decision, take a brief pause if the situation allows. Put the decision into one sentence. Identify what is known, what remains uncertain, and when a response is actually needed.

Choose the smallest next action that improves the situation: clarify the request, gather a missing fact, prepare the conversation, or make the decision within an agreed boundary.

Afterward, review what happened. Was the original interpretation accurate? Did the action improve the outcome? What would have made you better prepared?

Over time, those observations can reveal a recurring pattern that is difficult to see from inside a single demanding moment.

What are you treating as a fact that is still an interpretation?

The same inquiry applies to the week around the decision. If your better judgment keeps getting spent on work that should not require it, read the calendar review for founders.

Research behind the idea

Amy F. T. Arnsten (2009), Stress signalling pathways that impair prefrontal cortex structure and function, Nature Reviews Neuroscience. The decision prompts above are an advisory practice, not a validated clinical intervention.
cta: If important decisions keep meeting you in the wrong state or with the wrong information, we can examine the person, the work, and the conditions together.
